mstts:express-as.prosody: Imagine the thunder of engines, the smell of leather, and that wild sense of freedom you only find tearing down an open highway. That’s the world you’re about to step into—one that pulses at the core of Hell's Angels, brought to life by Hunter S. Thompson. Together, we’ll dive into the story of a notorious motorcycle gang—feared by some, mythologized by others, and always living on the edge. What happens when society’s rules don’t quite fit, and a group like the Angels decides to make up their own? We’ll ride along as rebellion and lawlessness start to blur, and watch as these outsiders challenge everything mainstream America thought it understood in the 1960s. Get ready to experience the raw energy of a generation searching for meaning—caught up in counterculture, danger, and the quest for identity. We’re talking wild rides, explosive parties, and those adrenaline-fueled clashes with authority that seem to define an era. But beneath the chaos, there’s a deeper story—one about loyalty and alienation, about what it means to chase authenticity in a world that doesn’t always make sense. Through Thompson’s fearless reporting and close encounters, we’ll get to peel back the layers, separating myth from reality. So, as we set out on this journey together, expect to uncover the true face of a brotherhood that both fascinates and unsettles. We’ll explore freedom, fear, and what happens when the American dream goes completely off the rails. Ready to see where the ride takes us? Let’s jump in.

Chapter One: Drifting to the Edge — The Rise of the Outlaw Biker
Have you ever felt that restless energy, like the world around you is just a little too neat, too predictable?
Right after World War II, that feeling was almost in the air. Factories were humming, suburbs were popping up everywhere, and everyone seemed to be chasing the same version of the American dream. But not everybody felt at home in that new normal. Some folks just couldn’t shake the sense that they were living by someone else’s rules.
That’s the world where the outlaw biker was born. Not some comic book villain, but a real person searching for something more than a steady paycheck and a white picket fence. The Hell’s Angels—yeah, that name would soon be everywhere—started out as just a bunch of guys who found meaning in the roar of a motorcycle and the freedom of the open road.
These weren’t rebels just for the sake of rebelling. Many of them had served in the military, came home, and found that the world they’d fought for didn’t really have a place for them anymore. The brotherhood they’d known in the barracks? Gone, replaced by a society that didn’t seem to care about their restlessness.
In the beginning, the Angels were just one of many motorcycle clubs scattered across California. Their get-togethers were rowdy, sure, but nothing legendary. They rode, they drank, and they built their own kind of family—something that felt a lot more real than anything on offer outside. Even their bikes became symbols: loud, bold, and impossible to ignore. They let the world know they were there, in a society that seemed to prefer silence and staying in line.
But as the club grew, so did the stories. Some of them were true, a lot were blown way out of proportion—tales of wild parties, fights, and trouble with the law. The Angels didn’t run from it. If anything, they wore that reputation like armor. The more people flinched, the more the Angels leaned into it. Being feared, being misunderstood—it became a badge of honor.
For most members, joining the Hell’s Angels wasn’t about breaking the law. It was about finding a place to belong, a tribe where loyalty meant everything. There were rituals—patches carefully sewn on jackets, engines roaring at sunrise, unspoken rules about how to ride. From the outside, it might’ve looked like chaos. On the inside, there was a strange kind of order.
Of course, there was always tension bubbling underneath. That line between true freedom and outright lawlessness? The Angels danced right on it, with a swagger that drew some people in and scared others away. Some wanted to push the limits; others just wanted to escape the daily grind. The club became a home for anyone who felt out of step with the world.
As the ’50s rolled into the ’60s, the Hell’s Angels stopped being just a local curiosity. Suddenly, they were the face of everything that unsettled mainstream America—defiance, unpredictability, and a refusal to just blend in. The media picked up the story, and soon, the legend of the outlaw biker had a life all its own.
But here’s something to pay attention to—most people never saw what really happened behind those headlines. They missed the long hours spent working on bikes, the quiet moments of friendship, and that complex mix of pride and frustration that kept the Angels coming back. All they saw was the danger, the threat to peace and order. The truth, as usual, was way more complicated.
The rise of the Hell’s Angels isn’t just about a motorcycle gang. It’s a mirror for a society tangled up in its own contradictions—a place where freedom and order are always pushing against each other. For those riding with the Angels, the road felt like salvation. For everyone else, it was a warning that not everyone was willing to play by the rules.

Chapter 2: Inside the Brotherhood — Rituals, Loyalty, and the Code
Stepping into the world of the Hell’s Angels? It’s a bit like crossing an invisible border. Suddenly, all the familiar rules fade away. The language changes, the markers of status and respect—everything you once thought mattered—just doesn’t count here.
The very first lesson for anyone drawn to this world is loyalty. Not bravado, not violence, not even the bikes. Loyalty comes first. Everything else? That can wait.
The Angels live by a code that’s simple, but absolute: the group comes before anything else. It’s not just some catchy slogan—it’s the way they breathe, the way they move. When you’re new, you learn fast that trust isn’t handed out. You have to earn it. There are rituals for just about everything—patches given for loyalty, silent nods that quietly welcome you in, and these unwritten rules about who gets to speak and who’s expected to just listen.
The hierarchy is clear, but it’s not about who’s got money or a fancy education. Here, respect gets measured in miles ridden, in risks you’re willing to take, and whether you’ll stand by your brothers, no matter what.
Now, if you’re on the outside looking in, these rituals might seem strange—even a little threatening. But for those inside, they’re everything. They’re the glue that holds it all together—a sense of belonging you just can’t find anywhere else. The world outside the club? It can feel cold, indifferent. But inside, there’s family. Members look out for each other—sometimes, maybe, a bit too much. Disputes get settled within the group, and trust me, outsiders are rarely invited in.
There’s one story that sticks with me—a young guy, just drifting from job to job, searching for somewhere to fit in. He didn’t really want trouble; he just wanted to belong. The initiation was brutal—endless rides, constant tests of loyalty, pressure around every corner. But when he finally earned his patch? The pride was overwhelming. For the very first time, he felt truly seen.
The Angels’ gatherings are a wild blend of chaos and order. There’s laughter, music, and that never-ending rumble of engines. But make no mistake—there’s discipline. Some topics are off-limits, and disrespect? That’s just not tolerated. If an outsider stumbles in, they’re usually shown the door—sometimes with a warning, sometimes with something a little stronger.
That code stretches far beyond the clubhouse. On the road, members ride in formation, each one knowing exactly where they belong. There’s this silent agreement: if one member’s in trouble, the rest follow—no questions asked. It’s a bond that’s nearly unbreakable, but it can be a double-edged sword. One mistake by a single member? Suddenly, it’s everyone’s problem.
When violence happens, it’s almost never random. It’s usually a response—a way to defend the group’s reputation or deal with a threat. The Angels are always aware of how the outside world sees them, and they protect their image fiercely. Sometimes that means going up against rivals; other times, it’s about disciplining someone inside who’s broken the code.
But here’s something to remember: for all the talk of toughness, there’s a softer side hidden underneath. Many members carry the scars of rejection—maybe from family, maybe from jobs, maybe just from a world that never quite knew what to make of them. The club becomes a kind of refuge—a place to hide those wounds, even if they never really heal.
So, these rituals and codes? They’re not just about keeping control. They’re about surviving in a world that often feels harsh and unwelcoming. For those who find a home within the club, the price of admission is steep, but what they get—a sense of purpose, belonging, and identity—makes it all worth it.
Most people never see this side. They just see the headlines—never those quiet moments of loyalty and trust that keep the brotherhood together.

Chapter 3: The Media’s Gaze — Sensationalism, Myth, and the Making of a Legend
Have you ever noticed how a single story, told over and over, can start to feel like the only truth? That’s exactly what happened with the Hell’s Angels. The media’s attention was a double-edged sword for them—part curse, part blessing. Their reputation didn’t just grow because of what they did, but because of how those actions were reported, and, honestly, how they were exaggerated and retold, again and again.
In the early days, unless you lived in California, you probably wouldn’t have even heard of the Angels. But almost overnight, that changed. Suddenly, newspapers and magazines were filled with wild stories—riots, assaults, chaos in the streets. The headlines were loud and clear: the Hell’s Angels were dangerous, unpredictable, and completely out of control.
But if you looked closer, the truth was almost never that simple. Many of these stories came from rumors, or from people who’d never even met an Angel. Some events got blown way out of proportion. Others? Made up out of thin air. And the Angels weren’t exactly innocent bystanders in this—they understood the power of a notorious reputation. In a way, they used it to keep outsiders at arm’s length.
There’s one incident that really sticks out. Picture a small-town festival turning into what the papers called total mayhem—motorcycles tearing down the streets, locals running for cover, police helpless to stop it. But if you talk to people who were actually there, you get a different story. Sure, there was plenty of drinking and some rowdy behavior. But the violence? Nowhere near what was reported. What really happened was more about misunderstanding and fear than real danger.
The media’s obsession with the Angels created this wild feedback loop. The crazier the stories, the more coverage the Angels got. And that attention? It started to draw in new recruits—some looking for a thrill, others wanting their own taste of infamy. Pretty soon, the Hell’s Angels were both villains and antiheroes. They became symbols of everything that scared and fascinated mainstream America.
For most people, the line between fact and fiction just disappeared. Even if you’d never met a Hell’s Angel, you felt like you knew them—thanks to all those articles, photos, and TV specials. The outlaw biker became a sort of shortcut for rebellion, danger, and refusing to fit in.
But here’s something to keep in mind: behind those headlines, things were a lot messier. The Angels weren’t all the same—some chapters were rougher than others, and plenty of members were more interested in partying than crime. The media almost never made those distinctions. Instead, they lumped everyone together, turning the group into a single, menacing symbol.
And that had real consequences. Police crackdowns became more common. The public’s fear just kept growing. The Angels responded by pulling back, getting more insular, and trusting outsiders even less. It was a cycle—suspicion and sensationalism feeding off each other, making it nearly impossible for anyone to see what was really going on.
Most of us don’t realize just how much our perceptions come from the stories we hear. For the Hell’s Angels, the media’s gaze was both a spotlight and a cage. It lit up a few truths, but hid just as much. The legend kept growing, but the reality? That stayed just out of reach.

Chapter 4: Violence, Law, and the Boundaries of Freedom
There’s this constant tension running through the story of the Hell’s Angels—a back and forth between that deep desire for freedom, and the hard reality of violence. If you’re on the inside, the line between expressing yourself and crossing into lawlessness? It never stays still. It shifts with the moment, shaped by pride, circumstance, and sometimes just the need to survive.
The Angels have always insisted, "We're not criminals." But let’s be real—outsiders see it differently. Their reputation for violence didn’t just appear out of thin air. Sure, fights break out—sometimes over things that most people would probably shrug off. But inside the club, defending the group’s honor is a must. Using force isn’t just accepted, it’s woven into their code.
Picture this: it’s late, in a bar on the edge of town. A few harsh words, a little too much pride, and suddenly, there’s broken glass on the floor and police lights flashing outside. For the Angels, it’s another loyalty test—proof that no insult goes unanswered. But to the police? Well, it looks like one more threat that needs to be kept in check. The real truth? It’s tangled somewhere in the middle.
Law enforcement reacts with a mix of fear and frustration. There are raids, arrests, the whole system coming down like a sledgehammer. And what happens then? The Angels just get more secretive, more protective of their own. It turns into a cycle—violence and retaliation, each side convinced they’re in the right.
But honestly, if you look closer, there’s more to it than just crime and punishment. Underneath it all, it’s a story about feeling alienated. A lot of Angels come from tough backgrounds—poverty, broken families, a sense of being left out. The club gives them a way to grab some power back, to take control in a world that feels like it’s moved on without them. Violence becomes their tool, their language. It’s how they show strength, demand respect, push back against a society that doesn’t make much room for outsiders.
So where are the boundaries of freedom, really? For the Angels, they see themselves as the ones standing up for individual rights, refusing to fit into society’s mold. But here’s the thing—freedom comes with a sharp edge. It lets you express yourself, sure, but it also brings conflict right to your door. The law? It’s not just a rulebook—it’s a barrier, a challenge to get around instead of something to follow.
Most people don’t have to think about these boundaries. They stay inside the lines, trusting the system to keep them safe. But for the Angels, the system feels like an enemy—something trying to stamp out anything different. And when violence breaks out, it’s not just about breaking the law. It’s about fighting for the right to define what freedom really means.

Chapter 5: The Outlaw Image and the American Dream
There’s always been a strange fascination with people who live outside the rules. Think about the Hell’s Angels—the leather jackets, the thunder of their engines. They didn’t just break the mold; they became icons of rebellion. But it wasn’t just what they did, it was what they stood for. In a country built on the promise of freedom, the Angels managed to capture both the dream and the nightmare all at once.
For a lot of folks, the Angels seemed like everything that was wrong with the sixties—lawlessness, a total disregard for authority, and that sense that old values were falling apart. But for some, the story was different. The Angels symbolized a kind of purity—people who refused to compromise, who chose to live by their own rules, no matter what it cost them. The line between hero and villain? It was never clear.
You know, the American dream promises success and stability, but not everyone finds their place in it. The Angels were living proof that not everybody wants the same things. For anyone feeling left out by all that progress, the club offered something else—a chance to carve out their own space in a world that seemed to look right past them.
That image of the outlaw biker—it took on a life of its own. Movies, music, rumors—they all helped build the myth. And the Angels got it. They played right into the cameras, knowing every photograph, every headline, just made their legend grow. People saw what they wanted: danger, excitement, the thrill of breaking free.
But if you look behind the curtain, the reality was a lot more ordinary. Most of the time, the Angels did what everyone else does—working, arguing, trying to figure out what life’s all about. The real difference? It was in how they chose to live, that stubborn refusal to accept someone else’s boundaries.
This push and pull—the outlaw image clashing with the American dream—that’s the heart of the Angels’ story. It’s really about searching for meaning in a world that can feel empty, about wanting to belong but knowing there’s a price for standing apart. Most people never even have to make those choices. They just follow the path set out for them, trusting it’ll lead to happiness.
For the Angels, happiness isn’t handed over. It’s something you have to grab for yourself. The open road is both a shelter and a test—a place where rules are made and broken, sometimes at the same time. The dream of real freedom is always just out of reach, but maybe that’s the point. For them, the hunt for it becomes its own kind of salvation.

Chapter 6: The Road Unfolds — Journeys, Brotherhood, and the Open Highway
There’s a certain kind of magic that takes over when the world shrinks down to nothing but a strip of asphalt, and the horizon seems to go on forever. For the Hell’s Angels, the road wasn’t just a way to get from point A to point B. It was almost alive—breathing, shifting, inviting them into a space where the usual rules just... faded away. Something raw, something real, took their place.
Picture this: a long ride, engines humming in perfect sync, winding through small towns and stretches of desert that feel like they go on for days. The world outside the pack—well, it starts to feel distant. Almost like it’s not quite real. There’s a certain rhythm to these journeys. The ritual of stopping at a roadside diner. The laughter that bubbles up after hours of quiet. The way the group moves like a single being, every rider in tune with the others. For a while, all the baggage from the past and the worries about the future just slip away. There’s only the road ahead, and the simple act of moving forward.
Imagine this: dusk settling over the highway, and one rider drifts into his thoughts as the wind tugs at his jacket. He remembers his first ever run—the nerves, the excitement, that fear of not really belonging. But now, after all these years, the road actually feels like home. Faces around him may have changed, but that deep sense of belonging? It’s still there. For a lot of these guys, these rides became a kind of therapy. A way to work through pain, to find a real connection, and to just feel alive.
Of course, the road isn’t always gentle. There are breakdowns, accidents—moments where things get seriously dangerous. Sometimes, one wrong turn means running into trouble with locals or the police. That’s when the Angels really lean on each other. They have to trust that someone’s got their back, no matter what. And that trust? It’s not given lightly. It’s built, slowly, through all those shared experiences.
Most people never see this side of the story. They picture nothing but chaos and violence. But they miss the quiet moments—the cigarettes shared at dawn, stories swapped over a cup of cheap coffee, the way a small gesture can mean everything. The road, for all its risks, offers a kind of freedom you just can’t find anywhere else.

Chapter 7. Collisions with Authority — Trials, Tensions, and the Price of Defiance.
Every story about rebellion eventually hits a wall—and for the Hell’s Angels, it was only a matter of time before they collided with authority.
The more attention they drew, the harder police and politicians worked to clamp down on them. What started as a few scattered arrests? That quickly escalated into a full-on campaign to wipe out the club’s influence.
Raids became part of daily life. Imagine waking up to early morning knocks, watching your clubhouse get torn apart, or seeing your friends led away in handcuffs. The Angels got used to it—always looking over their shoulders, scanning for unmarked cars and undercover cops.
Some members started to see threats everywhere, thinking even strangers might be informants. Others just shrugged—after all, wasn’t this the price of living outside society’s lines?
There was one night, after a particularly rough run-in with the law, when a member found himself alone in his garage, replaying everything that had happened. He started to wonder—was it really worth it? The constant stress, the risk of jail, and that uneasy feeling when friends just disappeared without a word. But then, he remembered the rush of riding with the pack, the sense of purpose that came from being part of something bigger. For better or worse, this was his life.
And when it came to legal battles, fairness was rare. Prosecutors painted the Angels as monsters, pulling out every trick they knew just to win a conviction. Sometimes, the evidence was shaky—but all it took was public fear to tip the scales.
The Angels’ response? Close ranks. Refuse to cooperate. Make it clear: betraying the group carried a heavy cost.
Even with all this pressure, the club survived. Members came and went, but the core never really changed. The Angels learned to adapt—some chapters went underground, others tried to clean up their image. There was always that tension, though: defiance on one side, self-preservation on the other. Every choice was shaped by it.
Most people never have to think about what it feels like to be hunted, to live knowing the system’s stacked against you. For the Angels, that was just daily reality.
The price of defiance? It was high. But for many of them, it was a price worth paying.

Chapter 8: Outsiders and Allies — Women, Friends, and the Edges of the Club.
The world of the Hell’s Angels was never meant to be open. It was a tight circle, a club with walls high enough to keep just about everyone out.
But here’s something to consider—no group can really shut itself off from the world entirely, can it? On the fringes, there was always a shifting crowd. Women. Friends. Curious onlookers who just wanted to get a little closer to the action.
Women, especially, found themselves in a strange spot. Some were drawn in by the sheer excitement—the wild parties, the danger that seemed to stick to the Angels like a shadow. Others got swept up in relationships that felt like a wild ride—equal parts thrilling and risky.
The club made its rules crystal clear: women couldn’t be members, and their place was always secondary. Still, in those quieter moments—when the noise faded—real bonds formed. The kind of connections that didn’t fit neatly into any category.
There’s one story that stands out—a woman who spent years around the club. She remembered the pulse of those early days... the rush of being part of something forbidden. But she also remembered the flip side—the fear, the moments when things spun out of control, and the sharp edge of loyalty. For her, the club was both a safe haven and a cage. She could be herself, but she was always just a little bit on the outside looking in.
Friends and allies came in all shapes and sizes—an old army buddy here, a local shopkeeper there. Some just admired the Angels’ rebellious streak. You had business owners who’d quietly look the other way, lawyers who’d lend advice when it counted, even a few cops who—while they might not have liked what the club did—still respected their code.
But these relationships? They were always walking a tightrope. Loyalty could flip to betrayal in a heartbeat, and trust was slow to build—quick to vanish. The Angels learned early on to be careful about who they let in, and even more careful about who they forgave.
Life outside the club was unpredictable. The line between friend and enemy was always blurry. But every now and then, something real happened—a laugh shared, a hand offered in tough times, a brief moment when those heavy walls actually came down.
Most people never get to see this side. They picture the club like a fortress—impossible to break into, never changing. But if you look a little closer, you’ll see there’s more going on. The Angels, for all their tough talk, were shaped by the people around them. Loved, hated, misunderstood—but never truly alone.

Chapter 9: The Turning Tide—Change, Disillusionment, and the End of an Era
You know, no story ever stays the same forever. As the sixties faded into the seventies, the world around the Hell’s Angels started to shift—sometimes slowly, sometimes all at once.
The country was restless. War, protests, and a wave of cultural upheaval left almost everyone searching for new answers. And the Angels? They went from being icons of rebellion to feeling a little bit trapped—caught somewhere between what they’d been and whatever might come next.
Some members started to feel pretty disillusioned. That old feeling of brotherhood? It got harder to find. Instead, suspicion crept in, and even close friends began to look over their shoulders. The media, which once gave them power and a bit of swagger, suddenly became a burden. Every misstep was blown out of proportion. Every rumor, no matter how wild, started to sound like the truth. The reputation they’d built over the years—carefully, with pride—was now working against them.
Imagine being one of the old-timers, watching a new generation take the reins. There’s this pang of nostalgia for the early days... for the simplicity and sense of purpose that had once brought everyone together. Now, it felt like everyone was just looking out for themselves. The rituals were still there, but the meaning behind them? That was slipping away.
And outside the club, everything was changing too. Law enforcement was getting smarter, trying new tactics to infiltrate and break up the group. The public, once fascinated by the outlaw mystique, started to get tired of all the violence and chaos. No matter how tough or defiant the Angels tried to be, there was just no escaping the pull of time.
Yet, even as the old ways faded, something new started to take shape. Some chapters tried to adapt, reaching out to their neighborhoods, easing up on the violence, and focusing on the bonds that had always held them together. Others went the opposite way, doubling down on that outlaw image with even more intensity.
Most people never really notice how meaning can slowly erode—the way traditions become hollow when the world moves on. For the Angels, the end of an era was bittersweet. It was both a loss and a chance... a chance to redefine themselves, or maybe, just maybe, to fade into legend.

Chapter 10. Legacy and Reflection — The Outlaw Myth in Modern America.
Funny how time works, isn’t it? It turns real stories into myths—sometimes before we even notice. Decades after they first burst onto the scene, the Hell’s Angels are still more than just a motorcycle club. They’ve become a symbol—of rebellion, of freedom, and honestly, of what it really costs to live outside the lines.
Their story is stitched right into the fabric of American culture. It’s like a thread running just beneath the surface—a reminder of the tensions, the push and pull, that shape our country.
Think about it: the outlaw biker used to be a figure people feared. Now, in some circles, he’s almost a folk hero. Movies, books, and TV shows have turned the Angels into these larger-than-life legends. But when you look closer, the real struggles—the victories, the losses—they’re often hidden behind the haze of myth. The truth? Well, it’s always more complicated than the legend.
For some folks, the Hell’s Angels are a cautionary tale. They’re a warning about what can happen if you feel cut off from the world, if you push back too hard, or if you trust loyalty above all else. But for others, the Angels are something else entirely. They’re proof that you can carve out your own space—even if the world isn’t exactly welcoming.
There’s a story from a former member, now much older, looking back on it all. He remembers the rush of the ride, the deep sense of belonging, those moments when the connection felt real. But he also remembers the pain—the betrayals, and just how quickly the world could turn cold. Looking back, he sees that the Hell’s Angels’ story is really about what it means to be human. To search for meaning. To fight for a place to belong. To wrestle with the fallout from the choices we make.
Most people out there, well, they never have to face choices like these. They color inside the lines, trusting that the system will take care of them. But the Angels, with all their flaws, remind us that there’s always another way. It’s a path that’s tougher, riskier—but sometimes, it feels more honest.
When you get down to it, the legacy of the Hell’s Angels isn’t just about motorcycles and mayhem. It’s about the search for freedom. The need for connection. And the price we pay for both. Their story is a mirror—one that reflects our own hopes and fears, and the constant struggle to balance order and chaos, fitting in and standing out.

As we wrap up this journey into the world of the Hell’s Angels, maybe you’re realizing this was never just a story about a motorcycle club. It’s really a window into the restless spirit of a whole generation—the longing for meaning, the push and pull between wanting to belong, and needing to be free. The Angels’ story isn’t just headlines and outlaws—it’s about the choices we all face when our world feels too tight, and the risks we’re willing to take to find where we truly fit. So, what can we take away from their ride on the edge? Sometimes, true belonging comes with a cost, but the rewards? They can be life-changing. The line between freedom and chaos? It’s a lot thinner than most of us think. Myths are powerful, but the real stories—messy, complicated, deeply human—mean so much more. Loyalty can protect you, but it can trap you, too, depending on how you hold onto it. And the search for meaning? That’s something we all share, even if we take very different roads to get there. If you ever find yourself drawn to the edge, questioning the rules, or just searching for your place, remember—every path asks something of us. The Hell’s Angels show us that rebellion isn’t just about breaking laws; it’s about the guts to live honestly, even when the world pushes back. Their journey is a reminder of how powerful community can be, how tough isolation feels, and just how much we all want to be seen and understood. And you know, you don’t need a bike or a patch to feel that pull of the open road. The real lesson here is about daring to live on your own terms, finding your people, and holding tight to what matters most—even when others don’t get it. So as you head back into your own life, maybe ask yourself—what do freedom, loyalty, and belonging mean to you? Because the road’s always open, and your journey is just waiting to begin.
